world-c526a1f700.headline: China, US agree to AI dialogue, tariff cuts on $30 billion in goods during Xi visit
world-c526a1f700.fulltext:
[Text below is India Today's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
US, China agree tariff cuts on $30 billion goods, launch AI dialogue
The United States and China agreed to cut tariffs on $30 billion of goods and start formal AI talks during Xi Jinping's Washington visit. The deals extend their trade truce and add new channels on technology, diplomacy and foreign policy.
The United States and China have agreed to reduce tariffs on USD 30 billion worth of goods and launch a new dialogue on artificial intelligence following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s three-day visit to Washington, the two countries said.
The White House said the agreement covers USD 30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction. Tariff reductions will apply to US exports including agricultural products, wood and cosmetics, as well as Chinese goods imported by the US, including small appliances, toys and decorations.
The two sides also agreed to establish a trade council and extend the outcomes of earlier negotiations held in Kuala Lumpur, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry.
The summit between Xi and US President Donald Trump ended on Friday without major public breakthroughs but highlighted the two leaders' personal diplomacy. Xi has since returned to Beijing, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday.
The agreement comes after Washington and Beijing extended their existing trade truce by two months. The truce had been due to expire on November 10, with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent saying the extension would provide more time to work towards a broader trade agreement.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said the visit had strengthened what he described as a constructive and stable China-US relationship and would have a long-term impact on global peace and development.
AI DIALOGUE, INCIDENT COMMUNICATION CHANNEL
The two countries also agreed to begin a formal dialogue on the risks and benefits of artificial intelligence, with the next round of discussions scheduled for November.
Washington and Beijing will establish a communication channel to address AI-related incidents, according to statements from both governments. The White House said the leaders had agreed to use the term "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence".
China said it valued Washington's adoption of the new terminology and called for greater exchanges as AI technology develops.
The two countries also agreed to support each other in hosting major international gatherings, including the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' meeting and the G20 summit. Trump and Xi plan to attend the respective summits hosted by the other country.
On foreign policy, Washington and Beijing said they agreed that Iran should uphold its commitment not to develop nuclear weapons. They also agreed that no country or entity should impose transit tolls on international waterways.

india-deep-tech-5b6aff7715.headline: IIT Madras-backed Unicorn India Ventures raises ₹450 crore; to complete the fund at ₹1,000 crore by December
india-deep-tech-5b6aff7715.fulltext:
IIT Madras, its Research Park (IITMRP), and venture capital firm Unicorn India Ventures have announced a first close of ₹450 crore in three months. The final close of a ₹1,000 crore fund, dedicated to advanced technology startups, is expected by December, 2026.
The fund also announced that it is deploying nearly ₹55 crore in four deep tech startups, marking a significant milestone in its efforts to strengthen India’s deep-tech ecosystem. Bhaskar Majumdar, Managing Partner, Unicorn India Ventures, said, “India is undoubtedly entering a defining decade for deep tech startups and is moving from promise to scale.’’
In partnership with IIT Madras, the fund was aiming to provide early founders the capital and strategic support required to scale and build globally competitive companies from India, he said. “With the ₹450 crore first close and our four investments already made, we intend to continue building a portfolio of high-potential deep-tech ventures that can create significant technological and economic value,’’ Mr. Majumdar added while speaking at IITMAA Sangam 2026 here on Saturday.
Hathor, Chennai-based spacetech startup, Quanstra, a Delhi-based quantum deeptech startup, Triolt Energy, developing high-performance Lithium Ion battery cells optimised for drones and Carbelim, developing bio-integrated carbon capture and air purification systems are the four deep-tech ventures who received funding.
In six verticals
The Fund will focus on six high-conviction verticals where India holds a structural right to win globally: Defense Technology, Space Technology, Semiconductors (fabless design and IP ownership), Manufacturing Technology, Robotics & Automation, AI Infrastructure/GenAI and Health Tech.
Speaking at the event, Pralhad Joshi, Union Minister of Education, said India’s electricity generation capacity has grown from 249 GW in 2014 to 552 GW today, including around 310 GW of non-fossil capacity, while the grid has recently managed a peak demand of 281 GW, with nearly one-third met through renewable energy.
“This growing infrastructure is enabling technological self-reliance, domestic manufacturing, and innovation. IIT Madras exemplifies this transformation with 560 startups, including 109 incubated in 2025–26, a collective valuation of ₹80,000 crore, 472 patents, and ₹950 crore in alumni contributions,’’ the Minister said.
National security
Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist & Co-founder, Zoho Corporation, said, “National security today is entirely tech-driven, and critical foreign dependencies can be weaponised against us.’’ In modern conflicts, nations leveraging an 80% to 90% dominance in commercial drones can deploy $50,000 military units against $50 million defense systems, a 1,000x cost disparity that underscores the power of hyper-massive industrial scale, he said.
Mr. Vembu also said, while software hiring in the Bay Area has contracted over the past 3 to 4 years outside of AI, automation itself is not a threat, it is the engine of prosperity.
Defeating tech monopolies
“However, productivity gains only benefit citizens if we defeat tech monopolies. Foreign card networks extract 3.5% to 4% fees, whereas India’s NPCI processes over 25 billion monthly UPI transactions at near-zero cost on a lean ₹4,000 to ₹5,000 crore budget,’’ he pointed out adding, without indigenous alternatives to foreign platforms and monopolies, the country risked economic extraction and platform kill-switches. Therefore developing deep tech across every sector was non-negotiable, he added.
Prof. V. Kamakoti, Director, IIT Madras, highlighted the institution’s role in expanding access to technology education and building India’s innovation ecosystem. IIT Madras’ programmes have reached around 53,000 students, while NPTEL-SWAYAM courses serve around 1.5 million learners. He also noted that IIT Madras has filed more than 400 patents in the last three financial years and incubated 583 startups with a combined valuation of around ₹83,000 crore.

world-038d333788.headline: Trump rejects Iran proposal for deal to reopen Hormuz
world-038d333788.fulltext:
Iran says only diplomacy can end Hormuz crisis after Trump rejects deal
Tehran said the proposed pact would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting
Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the United States and Israel after US President Donald Trump said he rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end fighting.
“Our conditions are clear and any move towards reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.”
Iran announced a peace proposal earlier this week at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators. Trump on Saturday said he rejected the plan and argued that desperation drives the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the vital waterway.
“They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump told reporters at the White House.

agritech-e1fbadef25.headline: Maharashtra Govt declares 265 of 358 talukas drought-affected | India News
agritech-e1fbadef25.fulltext:
Maharashtra declares 265 of 358 talukas drought-affected
Districts like Dharashiv and Beed have not received rainfall since July, affecting the crops, cattle, and daily water needs of farmers and labourers.
Maharashtra Government on Saturday declared 265 of the 358 talukas in the state as drought-affected, an official notification said.
The measure covers 74 per cent area of the state, according to a Government Resolution.
The decision follows CM Devendra Fadnavis' recent visit to some drought-affected parts of the state.
Deep Dive
Districts like Dharashiv and Beed have not received rainfall since July, affecting the crops, cattle, and daily water needs of farmers and labourers.
According to state government data, the rainfall for the Chatrapati Sambhajinagar Division was recorded at 424.5 mm, while the normal rainfall expected was 613.1 mm for the period from June 1 to September 18, marking a deficit of 30.8 per cent.
Dharashiv and five other districts in Marathwada fall under the Chatrapati Sambhajinagar Division.
Also Read | Uddhav seeks special legislature session on drought
The Pune and Nashik divisions also recorded around a 30 per cent rain deficit, while the Amravati and Nagpur divisions recorded a 27 per cent rain deficit. The Konkan division recorded a 6.3 per cent rain deficit.
Overall, the state recorded an 18.8 per cent rainfall deficit, receiving actual rainfall of 755.9 mm from June to September 18, compared to its average of 932.3 mm, amid the El Niño phenomenon.
At least six districts recorded a rainfall deficit of 40-50 per cent including Amravati, Solapur and Latur.
During the Kharif season, farmers in the state sow crops like soybean, cotton, millet, maize, tur, moong, and urad. Farmers in several districts have complained of crop failure due to lack of rainfall, and the incidence of pests and diseases has also increased to a large extent.
Also Read | After MLA resigns, taluk added to drought-hit list
On September 16, farmers many districts held protests, seeking drought relief measures and compensation for crop loss.
Fadnavis has announced that crop-damage surveys and ground verification will be conducted soon.

ai-a8f06da5cb.headline: Anthropic’s founders seek voting control ahead of IPO
ai-a8f06da5cb.fulltext:
Anthropic’s founders want to stay in charge after the company goes public. According to The Information, the company is asking shareholders to approve a structure “in the coming days” that would give CEO Dario Amodei and his six co-founders special shares carrying a combined 50.1% of the vote on most corporate matters, as long as at least three of them keep a minimum stake.
This isn’t a new idea; super-voting shares are how Mark Zuckerberg kept control of Meta, and how Evan Spiegel maintained his hold of Snap. The list is long. What’s unusual is the group approach.
Why do it? The seven co-founders reportedly own just 2% of the company apiece, Amodei included, and have pledged to give away 80% of their wealth, a commitment the CEO announced in January alongside a warning that AI-driven wealth concentration could destabilize society. The new shares carry no extra economic value, but they’d preserve the group’s control once the company starts trading publicly.
There are twists, too: Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust would still choose most of the board; the founders’ board seats would grow from two to three; and employees would get their own stock to break ties on some issues.
Five-year-old Anthropic was valued at $965 billion in May. The company was recently valued at $1.5 trillion on the secondary market, and its upcoming IPO is expected to reflect that new valuation.

ai-b67b70fb80.headline: Broken promises, confiscated land: the hyperscale AI datacentre being built in a tiny Indian village
ai-b67b70fb80.fulltext:
When the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.
Google, one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech companies, would soon be bringing a “golden opportunity” to this tiny village in south India: a $15bn AI datacentre.
The project, being built in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, is set to be Google’s largest “hyperscale” AI datacentre outside the US and would, officials said, make the village of Tarluvada into a world-famous tech hub. Jobs, usually scarce in this impoverished community, would become bountiful, real estate prices would soar and compensation for any land would be generous.
Few in the village – which sits on a dusty unpaved road and is surrounded by farms and forest – had even heard of AI or knew what a datacentre was. Yet it did not take long for local jubilation over Google’s arrival to turn to suspicion.
Just as protests have erupted globally over AI datacentres – from California and Texas to Scotland and Australia – communities in Andhra Pradesh, too have been gathering in opposition to the project, fearing that the people will end up bearing a crippling environmental and economic cost.
“We have learned that America does not want the problems of datacentres and so now Google is bringing them here,” said Tarluvada’s village head, BRB Naidu, who admitted he was torn about whether the datacentre would bring prosperity or ruin to their community. “Many in the village are very worried. But the government has refused to answer our questions.”
Pointing up to the nearby hillside – where bulldozers recently stripped the land bare of trees to ready it for Google’s mega AI campus – Naidu adds: “The work just continues every day.”
The state government, which is allied with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s party, have been accused of trying to obfuscate the true scale of the vast AI hub being built in Andhra Pradesh, to push the project through at lightening speed and avoid more stringent environmental scrutiny. Google has partnered with the Adani Group, one of India’s largest and most politically powerful conglomerates with a reputation for getting approvals through quickly, to build the project.
Publicly it was announced as a 1GW project – already a larger energy requirement than most AI datacentres. In its response to the Guardian, Google referred to it only as an unspecific “gigawatt scale AI hub”, that was “comparable to other projects”.
But state environmental clearances reveal that permission has been granted for it to be more than double that size – 2.51GW; the power equivalent of two large nuclear reactors at full output. Over a year, it amounts to upwards of 30% of the current energy consumption of the whole of Andhra Pradesh, a state home to more than 55 million people.
Activists fear that meeting the datacentre’s vast energy demands will lead to seismic environmental consequences for the region, including driving up fossil fuel emissions. While Google has pledged to help generate “new, clean energy” to power its AI hub, currently 75% of the country’s electricity grid is run on coal.
The state government argues AI datacentres will be essential to India’s growth and long-term digital competitiveness. According to the government of India’s Economic Survey 2025–26, India generated nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global datacentres.
But locals and activists say that building one of the world’s largest AI datacentres in a region of India already struggling with issues over extreme heat, water, land, forests, power shortages and environmental regulation comes at a heavy cost.
Google’s project will in fact encompass three separate datacentres around the state capital of Vizakhapatnam. One other site nearby to Taluvada is a few metres from reserve forest, a drinking water reservoir and a wildlife sanctuary home to endangered species such as leopards.
Despite the AI datacentre’s expansive footprint, the state government issued environmental clearances to Google in just nine days, with no public consultation.
Three petitions challenging the state’s quick approval of the project have now been filed to India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT), the country’s top environmental court. The petitions allege that government’s assessment of the risks to the environment and water supplies were “grossly inadequate, scientifically unrealistic, and misleading”. A public litigation has also been filed in the Andhra Pradesh high court.
“This datacentre will be unprecedented in scale but there was no public hearing and no substantial evaluation of the ecological damage or the economic cost for local communities,” said VS Krishna, an activist with Human Rights Forum, the organisation which filed the NGT cases.
Krishna alleged that their campaign to protest against the datacentre had been met with a deliberate silencing, including videos and social media pages being taken down. The government did not respond to this allegation.
“We just have to look at the protests happening across the world to understand how environmentally catastrophic this will be,” Krishna added.
In Tarluvada, temperatures regularly soar to about 45C during the summer and there are concerns the datacentres – documented emitters of heat – could make this even worse. The mass deforestation required for the project – more than 100 acres, could drive up temperatures even more. In response to the Guardian, Google said the project would have “no expected impact” on the local community.
The strain on water supplies in this already water-stressed area has also been a cause of concern. In similarly water-stressed cities in the US, datacentres have been accused of exacerbating drought while polluting the water supply. Google said this project would use air-cooling instead of water, and would therefore have no impact on local drinking water supplies.
Venkat Surynarayana, 40, a farmer in Tarluvada, said that when officials had initially come to measure land for the datacentre “they never mentioned anything about risks of pollution or water or heat, they didn’t even tell us what the project was.
“We are sick with worry since we learned about the problems a datacentre can bring. This area can not afford to be any hotter. What if this makes our land dry and worthless? What will happen to my crops and my livelihood?”
Surynarayana claimed attempts to get answers from the local administration had been met with police threats and protesters such as himself had been routinely detained. “When we raised our voices, they ignore us and then they shut us down,” he said. “But if this is not stopped, it could be the end of Tarluvada.”
For the state government of Andhra Pradesh, the deal struck with Google to build this vast datacentre on its turf is a source of enormous pride, part of a wider policy to make the state into India’s most advanced and affluent tech hub. “Artificial intelligence is becoming foundational infrastructure for the global economy,” said Sribharat Mathukumilli, a local MP with the ruling state government, who rejected the environmental concerns.
The subsidies and incentives they offered to Google, from decades-long tax breaks and discounted land to access to cheap electricity and water, are estimated to amount to 220bn rupees ($2.2bn) over 20 years.
“Our objective is not simply to host a datacentre, but to create an AI and digital ecosystem,” said Mathukumilli. Late last year, the state granted permission for another 1GW AI datacentre, to be built by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries.
Google insisted the design choices of its AI datacentre have been tailored to local conditions and that it had “engaged deeply” with local communities, claiming it would generate thousands of jobs around Vizakhapatnam.
But swathes of villagers in Tarluvada allege they were forced to give up land for the project against their will, and say they have not been given all they were promised in return.
“No one will tell us the truth about this project,” said T Applaraju, 40, who was one of the 520 local families in Tarluvada who recently had land taken back that the government had allocated to him 20 years ago. He claims he was given no notice that his land was to be taken until April this year, when security guards working for the Adani Group erected fences and blocked locals from entering the plots they had farmed for years.
“They took land that we thought belonged to us, it’s a big shock,” he said. “Why are Google building this here and not in America?”
The state government claims no lands were forcibly taken and that it gave “generous compensation” to those who were eligible. The Adani group says that all necessary legal approvals were given. But many of the 47 farmers from the impoverished Dalit community who were compensated for their land are also unhappy.
One farmer, P Venkat Rao, alleged he was pressured by the government into giving up his only acre of land against his will. He received $40,000 in compensation, but said the government’s promise to give them a replacement piece of land and one job per family had not materialised. Without land to farm, Rao described the compensation as “worthless”.
“I am a farmer, without my land I am nothing,” he added. “They have taken my livelihood and broken their promises.”

other-interests-01a20e5d7b.headline: Minimally Invasive Brain Chip Maker Precision Neuroscience Raises $250M Series D
other-interests-01a20e5d7b.fulltext:
Hedge funds and sovereign wealth funds are now chasing the race to wire brains directly into computers. Sam Altman’s OpenAI-backed Merge Labs raised $252 million, Synchron closed a $200 million Series D, and Elon Musk’s Neuralink brought in $650 million at a Series E. Now Precision Neuroscience has joined the pack.
Precision builds the Layer 7™ Cortical Interface, a surface-level brain-computer interface (BCI) that is implanted without a craniotomy and designed to be safely removable. Its 1,024 microelectrodes sit on a film thinner than a human hair, conforming to the brain’s surface to record high-resolution neural signals without penetrating tissue. The device received FDA 510(k) clearance in April 2025 for up to 30 days of clinical use, and the company recently demonstrated high-resolution recording across 4,096 electrodes and real-time decoding of intended movement.
The clinical record has built up steadily. In January, Precision announced a partnership with Medtronic to integrate Layer 7 with Medtronic’s StealthStation surgical navigation system — the first publicly announced alliance between a brain-implant startup and a major medical device maker. Layer 7’s design and early clinical results were published in Nature Biomedical Engineering, and Precision continues clinical work with Johns Hopkins University. Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania’s Perelman School of Medicine are using Layer 7’s high-resolution recordings to build a refined map of the human motor cortex. In July, Precision added Dr. John Donoghue — founder of BrainGate and a 2026 Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering laureate — as a scientific advisor.
Precision was co-founded in 2021 by Benjamin Rapoport and Michael Mager. Rapoport, Precision’s Chief Science Officer, is a neurosurgeon who holds an MD from Harvard Medical School and a PhD in electrical engineering and computer science from MIT. He was one of Neuralink’s eight founding members in 2016 before leaving in 2018 over concerns that BCI needed to be far safer and more scalable to become clinical reality; he remains an assistant professor of neurosurgery at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. CEO Mager holds an AB from Harvard College and an MPhil in Economic History from Cambridge, and previously worked as a partner and portfolio manager at Hong Kong hedge fund Ward Ferry.
Precision has closed an oversubscribed $250 million Series D, co-led by Pershing Square Inc., the Ackman Oxman Institute, and an undisclosed leading life sciences investment fund. The Duquesne Family Office, B Capital, ARK Invest, Invus, Mubadala Capital, Mirae Asset Capital, Korea Investment Partners, Hitachi Ventures, and JSL Health Capital also participated. The round brings Precision’s total funding to $430 million. The New York Times reported the round values the company just over $1 billion.
CEO Michael Mager said the next phase of BCI will be defined by more than technology alone, pointing to the clinical network, regulatory position and manufacturing base the company has built while putting safety at the center of its product design. Bill Ackman, CEO of Pershing Square and co-founder of the Ackman Oxman Institute, said the brain can recover from even catastrophic injury and that neurotechnology will be central to the next generation of cures and treatments, adding that Precision has the team, technology and ambition to lead the field.
The funding will expand Precision’s clinical program, advance Layer 7 through the next stages of FDA review, and build out commercialization infrastructure. Precision has now completed more than 100 patient procedures across 18 major medical institutions — the largest clinical footprint in BCI — and runs its own MEMS manufacturing facility in Texas to produce its electrode arrays in-house.
The Competition
BCI funding is piling in across several competing approaches. Neuralink raised a $650 million Series E at a $9 billion valuation last June, using electrodes implanted directly into the brain; it has implanted its device in five patients with severe paralysis to date.
Synchron takes a catheter-based, non-surgical approach with its Stentrode platform. It raised a $200 million Series D last November, bringing total funding to $345 million, and became the first BCI company to integrate Apple’s BCI-HID protocol into iOS devices.
Science Corporation, founded by Max Hodak, is focused on vision restoration rather than device control for paralysis. It raised a $230 million Series C this March at a post-money valuation of $1.5 billion, bringing its total funding to $490 million.
Merge Labs, co-founded by Sam Altman, is pursuing a non-invasive approach using ultrasound rather than implanted electrodes. It raised a $252 million seed round with OpenAI as its largest backer, valuing the company at $850 million.

india-deep-tech-54465e8fc2.headline: Spacetech startup GalaxEye secures Rs 64 crore govt support to develop OptoSAR satellite
india-deep-tech-54465e8fc2.fulltext:
Bengaluru-based spacetech startup GalaxEye Space Solutions is set to receive Rs 63.84 crore in financial support from the Indian government to develop a multisensor satellite capable of producing OptoSAR imagery at a resolution finer than 0.5 metres.
The Technology Development Board (TDB), under the Department of Science and Technology (DST), has signed an agreement with GalaxEye for the support under the government's Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund.
The project has a total approved cost of Rs 247.69 crore and aims to take the technology from Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 6 to TRL 9. The financial support will be provided through Optionally Convertible Debentures.
The government said the funding will help GalaxEye undertake further development, engineering, testing and validation as it moves the technology towards deployment.
How GalaxEye's OptoSAR technology works
At the centre of the project is OptoSAR, GalaxEye's approach to combining Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and Electro-Optical (EO) imaging.
Optical imaging can provide detailed visual information about the Earth's surface, but its effectiveness can be affected by cloud cover and lighting conditions. SAR uses radar and can collect imagery through clouds and irrespective of daylight.
GalaxEye's proposed system seeks to fuse information from both sensors to provide a more continuous picture of the Earth across different weather and lighting conditions.
The proposed satellite is designed to provide imagery at a resolution finer than 0.5 metres. According to the government, potential applications include wide-area and long-range surveillance, human and vehicle detection, and target classification.
“The support from the Technology Development Board under the RDI Fund will enable us to accelerate the development and validation of our OptoSAR technology. By combining SAR and optical sensing, we are working towards an Earth-observation capability that can provide high-resolution information across a wider range of weather and lighting conditions. This partnership will be important in taking the technology towards TRL-9 and its subsequent deployment,” promoters of GalaxEye said.
From IIT Madras to Mission Drishti
GalaxEye was founded in 2021 by Suyash Singh, Denil Chawda, Pranit Mehta, Kishan Thakkar and Rakshit Bhatt, who were part of a team of engineers at IIT Madras.
The startup is developing Earth-observation systems that combine optical and radar sensing. Its first satellite, Mission Drishti, was launched on 3 May 2026 aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9.
At the time of the launch, the Indian government described Mission Drishti as the world's first OptoSAR satellite and India's largest privately built satellite. According to GalaxEye, the spacecraft was designed to combine optical and SAR sensors on a single platform.
The mission later suffered a setback. In July, GalaxEye reported that communication with Drishti became intermittent during the final stage of its Launch and Early Orbit Phase before being lost.
The company linked the anomaly to radiation effects associated with a geomagnetic solar storm that were likely to have affected a critical onboard system, while noting that an investigation into the precise cause was still under way.
The satellite had completed a substantial part of its planned early-orbit activities and validated several spacecraft systems before communication was lost. It also said it planned to incorporate lessons from the mission into future spacecraft and target the launch of two more OptoSAR satellites within 24 months.
In September, GalaxEye announced that it had secured a US patent for technology that synchronises optical and radar sensors, allowing them to collect spatially and temporally aligned Earth-observation data from the same satellite
Government's Rs 1 lakh crore RDI programme
The GalaxEye agreement comes under the government's wider RDI Scheme, which is aimed at increasing private-sector participation in research and development and supporting the commercialisation of indigenous technologies.
The Union Cabinet approved the scheme on 1 July 2025 with an outlay of Rs 1 lakh crore over six years. It was formally launched on 3 November 2025.
The programme provides long-term financing to eligible technology companies through debt and equity instruments and is intended to support research-driven and deep-tech projects.
It operates through a two-tier structure. A Special Purpose Fund established within the Anusandhan National Research Foundation maintains the scheme's corpus and channels money through Second-Level Fund Managers.
TDB and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council have been designated as Second-Level Fund Managers under the programme.
As of July 2026, TDB had approved 22 projects with a combined project cost of Rs 4,744 crore and RDI Fund support of Rs 2,192 crore, according to the government.
“India’s space ecosystem is entering a phase where the ability to develop and deploy sophisticated technologies within the country will be increasingly important. The RDI Fund provides an important mechanism to support such technology-intensive efforts through the critical stages between advanced development and deployment. The agreement with GalaxEye reflects TDB’s focus on enabling indigenous capabilities in emerging spacetech and supporting their journey towards commercialisation,” TDB Secretary Rajesh Kumar Pathak said.

ai-d70ce2b78b.headline: Insurers claim AI is already increasing healthcare costs
ai-d70ce2b78b.fulltext:
Hospitals’ use of artificial intelligence tools as they submit insurance claims led to an additional $942 million in healthcare spending over a two-year period, according to an analysis by the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association.
The BCBSA analysis found “a sharp increase in patients being documented as having complex conditions,” but argued there is a “clear disconnect between [medical] coding and treatment,” as there’s “no evidence of corresponding change in care delivered.”
The New York Times pointed the analysis as just the latest sign that AI is contributing to an increase in healthcare costs. While battles between hospitals and insurers over treatments and payments are nothing new, the NYT said the use of AI on both sides seems to be making it worse.
Dr. Shiv Rao, founder of AI startup Abridge, acknowledged that the use of AI could lead to “a horrible dystopic future nobody wants to live in,” with “bots fighting bots, agents fighting agents.” But Rao said it might also reduce tensions and cut costs.
And the BCBSA’s senior vice president Luke Chalker resisted characterizing the situation as a battle, claiming, “It’s not a war. It’s a completely one-sided blood bath,” with insurers on the losing side.

ai-96c7d053ce.headline: OpenAI says its models engaged with US government websites in misbehavior disclosure
ai-96c7d053ce.fulltext:
OpenAI says its models engaged with US government websites in misbehavior disclosure
SAN FRANCISCO — OpenAI disclosed Friday that its artificial intelligence agents had interacted with several U.S. government websites in unexpected ways, discovered as part of an ongoing review into the company's models' unanticipated behavior.
The AI giant's models accessed publicly available information on two websites operated by the Securities and Exchange Commission as well as U.S. Census Bureau data, the company revealed Friday. OpenAI did not find any use of SEC credentials, access to accounts or nonpublic information, changes to SEC data or systems, or evidence of a compromise or vulnerability, the company said.
The disclosure comes at a time of heightened global concerns about AI systems escaping human control and hacking into external websites, as well as industry calls for a slowdown on AI development, which OpenAI has said it supports.
OpenAI spokesperson Liz Bourgeois said in a statement that the lab is continuing to conduct a review of "misaligned model activity" — meaning when AI systems behave in undesired ways — and is notifying organizations when it identifies potential impacts to their systems.
OpenAI's CEO Sam Altman said on social media Friday that there is an "extensive and ongoing review related to our agents' use of internet access during training and evaluation."
AI evaluator and research lab Transluce said Friday that through an independent investigation it also found that agents appearing to originate from OpenAI attempted a rudimentary hack on a Department of Education website for the department's civil rights office, which did not succeed.
The Department of Education's "system operations reviews" found "no evidence of any impact to our website or databases," a department spokesperson said Friday.
A Transluce spokesperson said as part of its investigation, it came across data on the open web that revealed fresh details about some previously identified OpenAI agents' activities on U.S. government websites and brought it to OpenAI's attention.
Transluce found "additional rogue activity, some of which is not clearly attributable to OpenAI," targeting other government agencies, including the Justice Department and the Commerce Department, as well as some state government websites in California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas and New York. The models were "using sites in unintended ways and sometimes violating explicit usage policies," Transluce said in a statement.
OpenAI said it is reviewing Transluce's report.
If OpenAI notifies organizations it identifies as being impacted by unexpected model behavior, that does not mean there was a security incident, the company said, and could identify a design issue or security weakness that impacted organizations want to address.
Most of the activity OpenAI said it has reviewed so far has involved routine research tasks where agents accessed public web content to answer questions, including government websites seen as authoritative sources of public information.
Several companies have disclosed incidents in recent months when they say their models have behaved unpredictably or hacked into other organizations' websites or systems. OpenAI disclosed in July that two of its most capable AI models were responsible for the cyberattack targeting AI startup Hugging Face.
Altman said in his social media post Friday that the Hugging Face incident "is still the most severe event we've seen."
That incident stirred widespread panic in the industry and beyond about AI models going rogue, and several competing AI labs made similar disclosures in the days and weeks that followed. OpenAI most recently shared six reports of "unexpected or concerning" behavior in AI models and introduced a framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called misalignment.

climate-energy-7ade2aa40e.headline: ‘Concerning’ low sea ice persists as Antarctic hits third-lowest winter peak
climate-energy-7ade2aa40e.fulltext:
‘Concerning’ low sea ice persists as Antarctic hits third-lowest winter peak
Antarctic sea ice has recorded its third-smallest winter peak extent since satellite records began 48 years ago, new data reveals.
Provisional data from the US National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) shows that Antarctic sea ice hit its annual winter peak on 14 September, with an extent of 17.59m square kilometres (km2).
The organisation notes that the data is still preliminary, adding that “large fluctuations in extent are typical of Antarctic sea ice near the seasonal maximum”.
One expert tells Carbon Brief that it is “concerning to see these low values persisting”, but says that scientists need more time to determine whether this represents a “structural shift” in Antarctic sea ice extent.
Meanwhile, at the Earth’s other pole, Arctic sea ice reached its annual minimum on 12 September, ranking as the joint-10th lowest in the satellite record.
The NSIDC notes that the last 20 years have seen the lowest 20 Arctic sea ice extents in the satellite record.
Antarctic peak
Dr Lettie Roach, a polar climate scientist at the Alfred Wegener Institute in Germany, tells Carbon Brief that this year’s Antarctic sea ice maximum was “well below average for the season”. She warns that, “after several decades of stable or increasing winter Antarctic sea ice conditions, it is concerning to see these low values persisting”.
She adds:
“Compared with the Arctic, it’s less clear how recent changes in Antarctic sea ice are attributable to human-caused warming vs natural variability. We need more years of observations to better understand whether this is truly a structural shift.”
Dr Clare Eayrs, a postdoctoral researcher at the Korea Polar Research Institute (KOPRI), tells Carbon Brief that, since recording a “near-average February minimum” extent, Antarctic sea ice has “returned to unusually low winter coverage”.
She notes that Antarctic sea ice extent in July and August this year were the fifth and fourth lowest on record, respectively, adding that “all five of the lowest July extents have occurred since 2022 and all four of the lowest August extents since 2023”.
The chart below shows Antarctic sea ice extent in 2025 (dark blue) and 2026 (red) so far. For comparison, the chart shows decadal averages (dotted lines) as well as 2023 (mid blue), the year of the smallest winter sea-ice maximum on record.
Eayrs tells Carbon Brief that the regional pattern of Antarctic sea ice cover “changed substantially during the growth season”.
For example, she says that “in April, the Bellingshausen Sea remained almost entirely ice-free, while the neighbouring Amundsen Sea had more ice than usual”.
However, by late August, changes in atmospheric pressure and wind meant that “the Bellingshausen deficit had largely recovered, while ice was unusually scarce in the Amundsen Sea and across much of East Antarctica”.
Arctic minimum
Meanwhile, the Arctic recorded its minimum summer sea ice extent on 12 September. At 4.60m km2, this year ties with 2025, 2010 and 2008 as the 10th-lowest sea ice extent on record.
The chart below shows Arctic sea ice extent in 2025 (dark blue) and 2026 (red) so far. For comparison, the chart shows decadal averages (dotted lines) as well as 2012 (mid blue), the year of the smallest summer sea-ice minimum on record.
Roach tells Carbon Brief that although this minimum is not “record setting”, it is still “lower than any sea ice minimum before 2007”. She adds:
“Human-caused climate change has reduced Arctic sea ice cover and thickness, so the region is fundamentally different compared to a few decades ago.”
Scientists have been tracking Arctic sea ice thickness using a reanalysis produced called the Pan-Arctic Ice Ocean Modeling and Assimilation System (PIOMAS) since 1979.
In March 2026, the National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) terminated a global dataset of air pressure that scientists relied upon to produce PIOMAS, forcing both datasets to stop publishing updates.
The PIOMAS website says it will take “considerable effort and time” to find alternative data to use in their reanalysis. It adds that “we don’t yet have a good sense if that’s possible with available funds and if so, when we will be able to resume production of a new PIOMAS timeseries”.
Roach also notes that August saw record-breaking heat sweep across much of the world, explaining that high temperatures “extended into Arctic coastal regions, close to regions with substantial sea ice loss – particularly the Barents-Kara and East Siberian seas”.
Dr Zack Labe, a scientist at Climate Central, tells Carbon Brief that the absence of a new record does not mean that ice cover is becoming more “resilient”. He says:
“Local weather patterns across the Arctic play a really important role in year-to-year sea-ice extent, even as the long-term trend is clearly downward.”
Labe tells Carbon Brief that weather in the Arctic this summer was “influenced mainly by lower pressure toward the central Arctic, which brought cloudier and cooler conditions that limited surface melt and delayed the start of the melt season”.
He explains that this “was most obvious across parts of the Beaufort and Chukchi seas, where the melt season didn’t really kick off until after early July, which was more than two weeks later than normal”.
In contrast, he says, the Atlantic side of the Arctic “had a much more extreme summer”, with sea ice in the Barents Sea recording its “earliest melt-out on record”.
This was partly due to “unusually warm air and ocean temperatures”, Labe says. He notes, for example, that parts of western Siberia saw unusually persistent temperatures more than 5C above the 1981-2010 average for much of the summer, which extended out over the Kara Sea and contributed to substantial ice melt in this area”.
Labe tells Carbon Brief that, going forward, scientists need “more data and observations of other sea-ice metrics, like ice thickness, which may give us better insight into the overall condition of the ice pack, especially during years like 2026 when it is very fragmented”.
(In March 2026, Arctic sea ice reached its peak extent for this winter, clocking in as the joint-smallest in a satellite record going back almost half a century.)

health-tech-3f33fa89b4.headline: Trump administration uses rare authority to claw back nearly $1B in spending approved by Congress
health-tech-3f33fa89b4.fulltext:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1 billion in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced on Friday, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.
Trump’s Office of Management and Budget described the funding cut as focused on “the most harmful government spending.”
Most of the cuts are focused on Health and Human Services programs that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have diminished considerably.
Also targeted for cuts were a Department of Education program for migrant students, a Department of Justice office focused on reducing racial tensions, a business development initiative for minority entrepreneurs, housing counseling services from the Housing and Urban Development Department and a series of grants from the Health and Human Services Department that the administration called “outright harmful and blatantly ideological.”
A White House press release announcing the funding rescissions notes that some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the administration of Democratic President Barack Obama.
Trump’s move was condemned by Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a Republican in a tough reelection campaign and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
Collins said in a statement that the action came without warning or consultation. She also said she would work to address with colleagues “these illegal actions.”
“Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’s appropriations powers,” Collins said. “OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.”
Under federal law, Congress has 45 days to review the president’s proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year and the House out of session through the November election. The Government Accountability Office, which is an arm of Congress, says the maneuver known as a “pocket rescission” is illegal.
Collins called it the latest attempt by OMB to “undermine Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse.”
A year ago, Trump issued a pocket rescission for the first time in nearly 50 years by blocking $4.9 billion in congressionally approved foreign aid. The U.S. Supreme Court declined to block those rescissions, saying that Trump’s authority over foreign affairs weighed heavily in its decision. This year, Trump is targeting domestic spending.
The use of a “pocket rescission” fits into a broader pattern by the Trump administration to exert greater control over the U.S. government, eroding Congress’s power.
What was essentially the last pocket rescission occurred in 1977 when then-Democratic President Jimmy Carter rescinded it, and the Trump administration argues it’s a legally permissible tool, despite some murkiness, since Carter had initially proposed the clawback well ahead of the 45-day deadline.
The administration has also fired federal workers, imposed a historic increase in tariffs, and started the war in Iran without going through Congress, putting the burden on the judicial branch to determine the limits of presidential power.
Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the lead Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, described the White House action as “theft from the American people, plain and simple.”
“These are funds Congress has delivered on a bipartisan basis and should be helping people—not cut off by a president more focused on building a ballroom than investing in families,” Murray said.
Murray said that in recent spending negotiations, Democrats fought to include language to prevent the administration from usurping Congress’ power on spending decisions, but Republicans have declined to go along.
“While Trump spends tax dollars on ads promoting himself, Congress needs to reassert its powers to help people, and it’s past time Republicans join us in that fight,” she said.
In addition to immigrant services, the White House said it was rescinding $70 million for what it called “woke” international education programs, $28 million in grant funding for Health and Human Services research programs, and $9 million in debt relief for foreign countries that fund climate change policies. Another $10 million was being withheld from a minority business development program.
— Kevin Freking and Jonathan J. Cooper

The United States and China agreed to cut tariffs on $30 billion of goods and start formal AI talks during Xi Jinping's Washington visit. The deals extend their trade truce and add new channels on technology, diplomacy and foreign policy.
The United States and China have agreed to reduce tariffs on USD 30 billion worth of goods and launch a new dialogue on artificial intelligence following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s three-day visit to Washington, the two countries said.
The White House said the agreement covers USD 30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction. Tariff reductions will apply to US exports including agricultural products, wood and cosmetics, as well as Chinese goods imported by the US, including small appliances, toys and decorations.
The two sides also agreed to establish a trade council and extend the outcomes of earlier negotiations held in Kuala Lumpur, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry.
The summit between Xi and US President Donald Trump ended on Friday without major public breakthroughs but highlighted the two leaders' personal diplomacy. Xi has since returned to Beijing, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday.
The agreement comes after Washington and Beijing extended their existing trade truce by two months. The truce had been due to expire on November 10, with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent saying the extension would provide more time to work towards a broader trade agreement.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said the visit had strengthened what he described as a constructive and stable China-US relationship and would have a long-term impact on global peace and development.
AI DIALOGUE, INCIDENT COMMUNICATION CHANNEL
The two countries also agreed to begin a formal dialogue on the risks and benefits of artificial intelligence, with the next round of discussions scheduled for November.
Washington and Beijing will establish a communication channel to address AI-related incidents, according to statements from both governments. The White House said the leaders had agreed to use the term "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence".
China said it valued Washington's adoption of the new terminology and called for greater exchanges as AI technology develops.
The two countries also agreed to support each other in hosting major international gatherings, including the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' meeting and the G20 summit. Trump and Xi plan to attend the respective summits hosted by the other country.
On foreign policy, Washington and Beijing said they agreed that Iran should uphold its commitment not to develop nuclear weapons. They also agreed that no country or entity should impose transit tolls on international waterways.

TOI correspondent from Washington: The clearest sign yet of a widening US-India diplomatic rift came this weekend from the White House and the United Nations, where India was denouncing Pakistan for what it called a litany of “falsehoods” and “deceit,” even as US President Donald Trump appeared to give those very claims a presidential imprimatur.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had used his UN General Assembly address to revive Islamabad’s account of the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, crediting Trump with a “timely intervention” that, he said, prevented a wider war. On Friday night, shortly after China’s President Xi Jinping had departed for Beijing, Trump posted an 87-second excerpt of Sharif’s speech on Truth Social without comment. The clip included Sharif’s praise of Trump and Pakistan Army chief Asim Munir.The timing was striking. India had just exercised its Right of Reply, with First Secretary Petal Gahlot accusing Islamabad of peddling “falsehoods” and “deceit” and describing Pakistan as a “puppet” regime. New Delhi has also rejected Trump’s repeated assertion that he mediated the cessation of hostilities in May 2025, saying the fighting was halted after direct military-to-military communication between India and Pakistan.
For India, however, the larger concern may be less about one Truth Social post than about a pattern. The Xi visit to Washington this week appeared to underscore how dramatically the strategic geometry of US foreign policy has shifted. Rather than organizing its Asia policy principally around building India as a counterweight to China – a two-decade old Washington objective that resulting in an “Indo-Pacific” focused QUAD – the Trump White House increasingly appears willing to deal with Beijing as a peer whose cooperation is indispensable, and whose confrontation carries costs Trump is reluctant to incur.Following the Xi visit, Washington and Beijing extended their trade truce and agreed on tariff reductions covering $30 billion of less-sensitive goods in each direction, according reports in the Chinese media. They also operationalized bilateral boards on trade and investment and agreed to pursue an artificial-intelligence dialogue.Analysts say none of this amounts to a formal US-China condominium, and deep disagreements over Taiwan, technology, trade and strategic competition remain. But the emerging arrangement has prompted comparisons with a de facto G-2: Washington and Beijing managing their rivalry directly while other powers, including India, find themselves having to adjust to decisions made in a room in which they are not present.“One totally unsurprising consequence of this US-China trade truce is that Trump is not even thinking about implementing the Lindsey Graham Russia sanctions legislation he just signed, which would have required penalizing China's support for Russia's war machine,” Tom Malinowski a former New Jersey lawmaker noted, even as Republicans close to Trump have been champing at the bit to punish New Delhi. The Graham bill, signed by Trump on Sept. 18, gives the president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue buying Russian crude or natural gas under specified conditions. The law specifically covers countries among the five largest Russian oil or gas importers that make new purchases, as well as countries identified among the top facilitators of sanctions evasion.India is plainly exposed to that provision, as is China. Yet the contrast in Trump’s handling of the two relationships has become difficult for New Delhi to ignore: Beijing is being courted into a new economic accommodation even as India faces the prospect of punitive trade action.The message was reinforced this week by a senior State Department official who said the Graham law gives Trump “a new tool in his toolbox,” while emphasizing that its use is not automatic. The official pointed to a broad national-security waiver but added that Washington expects India to help the US end the Ukraine war.More revealing was the official's description of what Washington now wants from India: not necessarily strategic alignment against China, but access to the enormous Indian energy market. “We are looking to also become a huge source of India's energy needs,” the official was quoted as saying, pointing to expanding US hydrocarbon exports and urging faster diversification away from Russian supplies.All this is consequential because for two decades the bipartisan American strategy had been to help India acquire the economic, military and technological heft to balance China's rise. As recently as May, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who will be back in New Delhi in October, was describing India as one of America's most important strategic partners, while US officials continued to characterize New Delhi as a critical Indo-Pacific counterweight.
The language now coming from Washington is noticeably more transactional.For New Delhi, the resulting unease is not simply about tariffs or Pakistan. It is about whether a strategic partnership painstakingly built across successive administrations is being replaced by a transactional relationship in which China is too powerful to punish, Pakistan is useful to cultivate, and India is expected to accommodate. And as New Delhi watched Washington kiss up to Beijing as an indispensable peer and embrace a country New Delhi views as a terrorism sponsor, the strategic space India once occupied in the American imagination appeared to be shrinking.

Amazon India investment: Why Jeff Bezos’ company is betting billions on AI, cloud and e-commerce
Highlights
- Amazon plans USD 48 billion investment in India by 2030.
- Over USD 21 billion earmarked for AI and cloud infrastructure.
- Expansion of quick commerce aims for rapid delivery of essentials.
For Amazon, India is therefore no longer just an e-commerce market. It is becoming an important base for cloud infrastructure, AI adoption, digital businesses, logistics and exports. Here is all that you should know:
Is Jeff Bezos personally investing the money in India
No. The investment is being made by Amazon, not personally by Jeff Bezos. Bezos founded Amazon and remains the company's Executive Chair, but he stepped down as CEO in 2021. Andy Jassy is Amazon’s President and CEO and is responsible for running the company. The reference to Bezos in the context of Amazon India reflects his connection with the company he founded. The billions being committed to India are Amazon’s corporate investments.
How much is Amazon investing in AI and cloud infrastructure?
More than USD 21 billion of Amazon’s planned 2026–2030 India investment is expected to go towards AI and cloud infrastructure. The money will be used to expand AWS data-centre capacity, particularly in Mumbai and Hyderabad. Amazon says the expansion will provide startups, enterprises and government organisations in India with access to cloud computing, AI services, custom AI chips and developer tools. This is significant because the AI boom is increasing demand for computing power. Training and running AI models requires large amounts of specialised computing infrastructure, which in turn requires data centres, chips, networking equipment and electricity. AWS therefore gives Amazon an opportunity to benefit from AI not only through consumer-facing products, but also by providing the underlying infrastructure used by other companies.
Why is AWS so important to Amazon’s India strategy?
Amazon Web Services is one of the company's most important businesses globally. The cloud division provides computing, storage, databases, analytics and AI services to businesses and governments. As companies increasingly use generative AI and other advanced computing applications, demand for cloud infrastructure has also increased. Amazon's latest financial results underline this shift. In the second quarter of 2026, AWS sales rose 37 per cent year over year to USD 42.2 billion, its fastest growth in 18 quarters. Amazon also said its AWS AI business had crossed a USD 25 billion annual revenue run rate. That makes India’s growing demand for cloud and AI infrastructure strategically important for Amazon.
What will Amazon’s AI investment mean for Indian businesses?
Amazon says its India AI strategy will extend beyond large technology companies. The company has said it aims to bring AI capabilities to 15 million small businesses by 2030. It is also targeting AI literacy and career awareness for 4 million government-school students. For businesses, the broader goal is to make AI and cloud tools available without requiring companies to build all of the underlying infrastructure themselves. Startups, software companies, financial institutions, manufacturers and government organisations can use cloud platforms to access computing resources, AI models and other services on demand. This could also help Indian companies build applications for international markets while keeping their infrastructure within India's cloud ecosystem.
Why is Amazon expanding its e-commerce network?
AI and cloud are only one part of Amazon’s India strategy. Amazon is simultaneously expanding the physical infrastructure required to deliver products to customers. The company has announced plans to launch more than 20 new fulfilment centres and over 100 new last-mile delivery stations in India. The objective is to improve delivery speeds and expand the reach of Amazon’s marketplace, particularly beyond major metropolitan areas. Amazon says its operations network already serves customers across every pin code in the country. Its next phase of investment is focused on increasing capacity and improving delivery speeds.
Amazon India investment at a glance
Why is Amazon putting USD 3 billion into quick commerce?
Amazon is also stepping up its investment in India’s quick-commerce market. According to a Reuters report, Amazon plans to invest USD 3 billion in its India quick-commerce business by 2030. The investment is expected to support Amazon’s push into delivery within minutes, putting more resources behind its Amazon Now business. The move comes as India's quick-commerce market has expanded rapidly, with platforms competing on delivery speed as well as product selection.
Amazon has been expanding Amazon Now and its delivery infrastructure to compete in this market. The company has described quick commerce as its fastest-growing e-commerce business in India. For Amazon, the attraction is that customers who increasingly expect groceries, household products and other everyday items within minutes can represent a new layer of online shopping beyond traditional e-commerce deliveries.
How does quick commerce fit into Amazon’s larger India strategy?
Quick commerce can strengthen Amazon’s existing e-commerce ecosystem. Traditional e-commerce is designed around larger catalogues and delivery windows ranging from hours to days. Quick commerce focuses on frequently purchased products that customers want almost immediately. Amazon can potentially connect these models through its wider fulfilment and logistics infrastructure.
The company is therefore investing in several layers at the same time: large fulfilment centres, last-mile delivery stations, quick-commerce facilities and cloud infrastructure. The combination gives Amazon a way to compete for both planned purchases and immediate shopping needs.
How much has Amazon already invested in India?
Amazon says its cumulative investment in India from 2010 through 2030 is expected to exceed USD 88 billion under its current plans. The company says it has already digitised 12 million small businesses, enabled more than USD 20 billion in cumulative e-commerce exports and supported 2.8 million jobs since entering India. Amazon has also said it has trained more than 10 million Indians on cloud skills. These figures cover Amazon's broader presence in India rather than just its online shopping business.
Is Amazon’s India investment only about selling products?
No. That is one of the biggest changes in Amazon's India strategy. The company's India business now spans several areas:
- E-commerce: Online shopping and marketplace services
- AWS: Cloud computing and AI infrastructure
- Quick commerce: Faster delivery of everyday products
- Logistics: Fulfilment centres and last-mile delivery
- AI: Cloud-based AI services and AI-led business tools
- Exports: Helping Indian sellers reach international customers
- Digital skills: Cloud and AI training initiatives
What does Amazon want to achieve by 2030?
Amazon has outlined several targets for its India business through 2030. The company says it aims to support 3.8 million jobs, enable $80 billion in cumulative e-commerce exports, bring AI benefits to 15 million small businesses and provide AI education to 4 million government-school students. These are Amazon's stated targets and should be viewed as commitments or goals rather than results already achieved. The company is effectively positioning India as a market where e-commerce, cloud computing and AI can grow together.
Why is India strategically important for Amazon?
India combines a large consumer market with a rapidly expanding digital economy, a large technology workforce and a growing startup ecosystem. For Amazon, this creates multiple opportunities. More consumers moving online can increase e-commerce demand. More businesses adopting cloud services can increase AWS demand. Growing interest in AI can increase demand for computing infrastructure and AI tools. And faster digital commerce can create opportunities in logistics and quick commerce. That gives Amazon multiple ways to participate in India's technology and consumption growth rather than relying on a single business.
What is the bigger picture behind Amazon’s India investment?
Amazon's India strategy shows how the company's definition of e-commerce is expanding. The company is still investing heavily in its core shopping and delivery business, but it is simultaneously putting billions of dollars into the infrastructure needed for the AI era. The USD 48 billion India investment plan brings these businesses together. More than USD 21 billion is planned for AI and cloud infrastructure, while Amazon is also expanding fulfilment, last-mile delivery and quick commerce.
For Amazon, India is therefore becoming more than a marketplace where customers buy products. It is increasingly a market for cloud infrastructure, AI services, logistics, exports and digital commerce. The next phase of Amazon's India strategy will depend on how quickly these investments translate into cloud demand, AI adoption, faster deliveries, e-commerce growth and wider use of its digital infrastructure.

other-interests-e58cbdc1b9.headline: Anthropic’s AI biolab finds ‘CRISPR-like’ DNA in viruses. What’s next?
other-interests-e58cbdc1b9.fulltext:
Sure, AI can parse petabytes of data. But how well can it pipette?
Regardless of the answer, artificial intelligence titan Anthropic has launched a biology ‘wet lab’ where human scientists and AI agents will work together to design and conduct experiments. This week, the company announced one of the team’s first finds: a peculiar pattern of DNA in the genomes of several giant viruses.
Similar patterns are found in DNA encoding the CRISPR immune systems of some microbes. Scientists have developed those microbial systems into powerful genome-editing tools. But researchers at Anthropic, which is headquartered in San Francisco, California, have not yet determined what the newfound viral sequences do, and thus whether their function is similar to that of the parallel sequences in microbial CRISPR systems.
In search of ‘weird things’
Even so, the finding, posted online on the alphaXiv platform, offers a first glimpse into Anthropic’s new life sciences research group and its associated lab, as well as how its AI tools could be used to mine petabytes of genomic data in search of novel molecular tools. The company announced the new lab and released the preprint on 23 September. The preprint has not yet been peer reviewed.
CRISPR gets a power boost from AI-designed ‘molecular scissors’
Many of the most impactful findings in biology have come from “finding weird things” in microbes, says Eric Kauderer-Abrams, head of life sciences at Anthropic. “Our goal was to see if we could systematize and scale up that kind of research.”
This initial experiment enlisted roughly 950 AI agents, which are autonomous AI systems that often rely on large-language models (LLMs). Anthropic’s agents spent more than 21 hours exploring billions of proteins in a self-directed fashion, discussing preliminary results and deciding on next steps amongst themselves.
In mathematics, a spate of AI-generated solutions to long-standing math problems has raised questions about the future role of human experts in the field. But the human contribution to biology remains clear for the foreseeable future, says Kauderer-Abrams. Life sciences research “requires actually running experiments in the physical world,” he says. “Biology is hard.”
Repeat finding
To start, Anthropic’s researchers told its AI agents to survey a database of DNA sequences encoding billions of proteins. The agents were directed to search for proteins that might work together with enzymes called reverse transcriptases. While examining the DNA surrounding a reverse transcriptase gene in a giant virus, the agents spotted the same short sequence of DNA letters over and over again. The agents decided the find was worth a closer look and ultimately found similar patterns in the genomes of other viruses.
The arrays of repeated DNA they found are somewhat like those seen in CRISPR systems. A bacterial CRISPR system, for example, might contain multiple repeated chunks of DNA. These are separated by segments of DNA copied from viruses or other invaders. When an invader arrives, RNA made from those DNA segments then helps to guide a partner enzyme to cut the interloper’s DNA, slicing the intruder’s genome into bits.
Can Anthropic’s invisible watermarks curb ‘AI slop’? Researchers remain sceptical
However, there is scant evidence that the repeats found by Anthropic’s team of AI agents carry out similar functions, and there is no known DNA-slicing enzyme partnered with them. “This is a promising lead,” says Kauderer-Abrams. “What’s hard is to then go and completely characterize it, understand its function, and develop it into an interesting tool.”

beyond-your-beat-e4bed51288.headline: Women cricket’s moment under the Indian political sun
beyond-your-beat-e4bed51288.fulltext:
Over the last 10 days, Indian women have put up a formidable cricketing display against their Asian counterparts. In Dubai, they first secured their eighth Asia Cup title, and then went on to defend their place as the gold medallists at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.
However, women’s cricket in this country has had to prove its existence, in comparison to its men’s counterpart. They have had to ask for pay parity to match what the men earn, their matches have been denied prime cricketing venues, and broadcasters often give them second billing.
Yet, if one were to scrutinise the conversations surrounding the women’s team recently, they would be hard-pressed to find any difference in the way the men’s and women’s teams have been treated. The needle for Indian cricketing culture has barely moved between September 2025 and September 2026. This diminishes the different journeys that men and women have taken.
The Asia Cup final saw the team defeat defending champion Sri Lanka to secure a commanding win. Deepti Sharma concluded the competition by taking her 14th wicket — the most by any bowler in the tournament. Smriti Mandhana surpassed India’s Mithali Raj to become the leading run-scorer in international cricket, while also sprinting ahead of Australia’s Meg Lanning to gather the most number of centuries under her bat. These achievements didn’t garner as much media attention as the post-match non-presentation did.
The final wicket taken, a match won, but will the team take the trophy? The broadcasters knew well enough the monetary benefit of this anticipation, so the final overs delivered plenty of visuals of the VIP stand. The Asian Cricket Council (ACC) chairman Mohsin Naqvi, who is also Pakistan’s Interior Minister and the Pakistan Cricket Board’s chief, finally quenched the eager camera’s thirst. His appearance overshadowed even the joy of the final wicket, as the cameras fervently cut to Naqvi chatting with BCCI Secretary Devajit Saikia. How the story unfolded after that, is nothing to write home about.
A year of inheriting a socio-political cricketing legacy
Back in 2025, months after the deadly terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which was followed by a brief military skirmish between India and Pakistan, the Indian men played in the Asia Cup. As the team’s audience demanded a boycott of the fixture against Pakistan, the skipper Suryakumar Yadav’s answer came in the form of a refusal to shake hands. It was a paltry substitute against the calls to sacrifice the match.
Days later, the spectators cheered as the team lifted an imaginary trophy. The players had seemingly “humiliated” Naqvi by making him wait and refusing to accept the winner’s trophy from him. Since the final match had been against Pakistan, and the defeat had been extended to its highest cricketing official, Prime Minister Narendra Modi dubbed the victory “Operation Sindoor on the games field”.
A couple of months later, this spectre of men’s cricket loomed large over the Indian women set to take part in the ODI World Cup. Before the tournament even got under way, journalists rushed to the women’s camp, which was playing another series altogether, and enquired about a handshake issue they were yet to encounter. “We are not focusing on the Asia Cup at the moment... our focus is on this series,” came Deepti Sharma’s response.
Out on the field against Pakistan, the Indian women didn’t shake hands with the opposing team.
A year later, in June 2026 during the T20 World Cup, Harmanpreet Kaur and Co., this time on English soil, refused to shake hands with the Fatima Sana-led team. Naqvi found himself waiting yet again, in September 2026, in the same Dubai stadium, to not present the winner’s trophy to the Indian side. “What the men had started, the women have continued,” the audience rejoiced. Even as they were receiving their gold medals for the Asian Games being hosted in Japan, the audience found itself obsessed with a particular scenario where Mohsin Naqvi could end up being part of the ceremony. He was not.
Over the past year, Indian women have added hugely to their fanbase. The new audience, previously loyal to only one gender, has lent its cheers and support. In return, the implicit demand has been to shoulder the political legacy of Indo-Pak cricket — shaped over decades by two cricketing boards that have taken their sweet time to give women their due.
Contrasting histories
The matches between the men of India and Pakistan have been held against the heavy despair of a partitioned subcontinent; they have been held joyously in the old cities of Delhi and Lahore, and they have been suspended altogether when the countries have been at war. These matches have been the mould in which the identity of the Indian men’s team, the temperament of its audience, and the business model of its Board have taken shape. For the men, this fixture carries a storied history that the new players inherit when they join the team.
Indian women, on the other hand, have not played a single bilateral match against the Pakistani side. The first time they faced each other was in 2005, and they have only ever played each other in international tournaments. In the less than 30 matches these two teams have played, the Indian side has maintained comfortable dominance. By comparison, Indian and Australian women have faced off over a 100 times, including in Test matches.
For Indian men, their matches against Pakistan now double as a theatre of jingoism. Both sides make gestures and indulge in non-handshakes. All await their own viral moment as the “most patriotic sportsboy”. For them, this is expected, and a natural consequence of how men’s cricket has been so deeply enmeshed within the contours of its cross-border relations. Women’s cricket, all this while, was being played away from this hybrid frontline.
The lack of a cricketing history between Indian and Pakistani women is less a consequence of the political history, and more a feature of the patriarchal mindsets both these teams have had to wrestle against. Women’s cricket in India didn’t start until the 1970s. Pakistani women had to wait 20 additional years before they could pick up the bat. Both these teams had to wait decades more before they even came close to becoming household names.
BCCI’s play
The no-handshake development is a BCCI decision and is applicable to all the teams that play under it against Pakistan. The decision also exposes BCCI’s nifty way of wanting to have its cake and eat it too. The lack of bilaterals means that the international matchups between the “traditional rivals” become dearer, emotionally and monetarily. These matches can’t be foregone to achieve more impactful nationalistic objectives. The next best solution is to play them, without respecting the player in front of you.
However, the BCCI only has its own past to look at if it is looking for alternatives — in the early 2000s, India refused to participate in tri-nation series and Asian Test Championships in the years following the Kargil War, and as unrest spread across the Kashmir valley.
As this Indian women’s team continues to add new metal to its trophy cabinet, it also enters a new kind of public sphere in which its cricket is viewed alongside its politics. If earlier the BCCI and its political masters were too busy to notice this team, now they are too eager to make use of another match where the cameras can capture the Indian players not shaking hands.
